analysis.one_liner: Raises the maximum Pell Grant for low-income students, paid for with higher taxes on wealthy estates.
analysis.headline: The bill to nearly double the maximum Pell Grant was never taken up by any committee or the House floor; it ended the session with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set the maximum federal Pell Grant at $13,800, up from the roughly $6,895 maximum in place, for low-income college students, and adjust it for inflation going forward. To pay for it, the bill would repeal the temporarily enlarged alternative minimum tax exemption for individuals and move up the expiration of the temporarily doubled estate and gift tax exemption from 2026 to enactment, so large estates would owe federal tax above a lower threshold sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income undergraduate students, who rely on Pell Grants to afford college without taking on as much debt, gain a substantially larger award. Colleges that enroll large numbers of Pell recipients would also receive more federal tuition dollars.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the maximum Pell Grant at $13,800 for the 2022-2023 award year — roughly double the maximum of about $6,895 then in effect — by adding the appropriation-funded amount on top of a fixed base [S3].

For 2023-2024 and later, the bill makes the $13,800 maximum the statutory baseline and adjusts it each year by the change in the Consumer Price Index, so the award would grow with living costs instead of requiring repeated congressional action [S3].

The CRS summary describes the bill as increasing the maximum federal Pell Grant award and paying for it by repealing the increased alternative minimum tax exemption and the increased estate and gift tax exemption [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households would bear the cost. Repealing the enlarged AMT exemption would raise the alternative minimum tax on some taxpayers with higher incomes, and ending the temporarily doubled estate and gift tax exemption in 2022 instead of 2026 would expose large estates to federal estate tax above a lower threshold several years earlier.

drawbacks.text: The AMT change would raise taxes on some taxpayers with moderately high incomes, not only the very wealthy, because the alternative minimum tax is a parallel tax calculation that individuals with certain incomes and deductions must run even if they owe no estate tax [S3].

Moving the estate and gift tax exemption's expiration up from January 1, 2026 to the date of enactment would give wealthy families no time to plan for the lower exemption, affecting large estates as soon as the bill passed rather than after a phase-in [S3].

A skeptic of Pell Grant expansion would note that the bill raises the award through permanent statutory changes while Congress separately sets the funded amount each year through appropriations, so the combined cost to the Treasury grows automatically with inflation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and concrete: roughly doubling the maximum Pell Grant would meaningfully cut the debt load of the lowest-income college students, and indexing it would end the annual fight over the award size. The cost is a genuine tax increase concentrated on higher-income households and large estates, which is the point of the design but also the reason the bill had a hard political road. The bill is straightforwardly drawn and the tradeoff is clear; the main weakness is that no second member of the House would cosponsor it, which in practice ended it before any scrutiny of the tax offsets could begin.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on May 27, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
No further action was ever recorded: neither committee held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and no version was introduced in the Senate [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors during the roughly seven months before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Higher-income households and large estates are better off, since the tax increases that would have funded the Pell Grant expansion — repeal of the enlarged AMT exemption and the earlier sunset of the doubled estate and gift tax exemption — never took effect. Colleges and low-income students did not get the larger awards.

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the maximum Pell Grant to $13,800 and pay for it with tax changes on higher-income households; recruited no cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party and was never voted on, so there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Large estates and the highest-income households
industries.note: The bill would have raised their taxes to fund student aid: repeal of the enlarged AMT exemption would raise the alternative minimum tax on some higher earners, and ending the doubled estate and gift tax exemption in 2022 instead of 2026 would make large estates pay federal estate tax above a lower threshold years earlier. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran directly against low-income students who would have received larger grants.

A larger Pell Grant is paid to students and spent on tuition, so colleges enrolling low-income students would receive more federal dollars. Their interest runs alongside students', though colleges are also the indirect beneficiaries of any grant increase that flows into tuition.

Grants reduce the amount low-income students must borrow, so a Pell Grant increase shrinks the loan volume on which lenders and loan servicers earn money. The bill's title itself frames grants as the alternative to student debt.
